newsitem.title: LEBANON: Bank of Lebanon gives forex market signal. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bank of Lebanon gives forex market signal. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]

text.p: The Bank of Lebanon on Thursday lowered its offer price for U.S. dollars on the Beirut foreign exchange market for the first time since introducing a bid-offer system five weeks ago.
It offered to sell (Corrects from buy) dollars at 1,559 Lebanese pounds after holding the level at 1,560 pounds since September 24 when it switched from a single mid-price quotation.

The Bank has several times lowered its bid price for buying (Corrects from selling) dollars since introducing the new system, dropping it from 1,557 on September 24 to 1,553 at Thursday's close and thus widening the spread from the original three pounds to six or seven pounds.
Dealers said the central bank's action was a good signal on the health of the Lebanese currency, which has appreciated steadily for four years under Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.
"This confirms the downward trend of the dollar/pound exchange rate," Talal Abou Zaki, foreign exchange manager at Bank of Beirut and the Arab Countries, said.
He said the inter-bank market was currently dealing at the lower end of the central bank rate, at 1,553, 1,553-1/4 or 1,553-1/2 pounds to the dollar.

"One week ago we dealt at 1,560, at the upper side, today at the lower end. The central bank is leaving it to the market, to demand and supply, to bid at the upper or lower end with a margin of six or seven pounds," Abou Zaki said.
"This is better than before because we have a free margin now for commercial banks to make a better profit," he added.
Another dealing room manager confirmed that the Beirut foreign exchange market was now developing mainly on the basis of inter-bank activity rather than central bank intervention.
"Before, the market was mechanical. Now there is trading and decision making involved," he said.
"Activity has been quite small but very positive in terms of inter-bank activity," he said of developments since the bid-offer system was introduced.
Abou Zaki estimated that daily activity on the market varied between $5-10 million and $10-15 million. The second dealer put it at an average $15-20 million, occasionally going much higher.
The market depended to a large extent on demand for Lebanese pounds for investment in government t-bills, and on demand for dollars by investors taking profits from t-bills on maturity, dealers said.
